subject: Computer Networking
title: SMTP — Sending Mail
description: A quick, practical guide to SMTP — Sending Mail.

hook.text: SMTP is the protocol that delivers email. It has been pushing messages since 1982.

buildup.text: Your client connects to the SMTP server on port 587. It authenticates, then sends the message.

discovery.text: SMTP uses simple text commands: HELO, MAIL FROM, RCPT TO, DATA. It's readable by humans.

twist.text: SMTP only sends mail. It has no concept of folders, read status, or inbox management.

climax.text: STARTTLS upgrades the plain connection to encrypted. Without it, your email flies in the clear.

punchline.text: SMTP delivers mail. That's all it does, and it does it well.

quiz.question: What port does SMTP typically use for email submission?

details.summary: Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is the internet standard for sending email. SMTP uses a series of text commands between client and server to authenticate, specify recipients, and transmit message content. It was designed in 1981 and remains the foundation of email delivery despite its age.
details.whyItMatters: SMTP is the engine behind every email you send. Understanding it explains why email works the way it does and why certain security concerns like spoofing exist.
takeaways: SMTP uses text-based commands to transfer email between servers
It was designed in 1981 and is still the email sending standard
SMTP originally had no authentication, enabling spoofing

faq.question: Why is SMTP still used after over 40 years?
faq.answer: SMTP is simple, universal, and works. Every email server speaks SMTP, making it the lingua franca of email. Security extensions like STARTTLS and authentication mechanisms have been layered on top. Replacing it would require universal coordination across millions of servers.

faq.question: How does SMTP handle authentication?
faq.answer: Original SMTP had no authentication. SMTP AUTH was added later to require credentials before sending. STARTTLS encrypts the connection. SPF, DKIM, and DMARC verify that servers are authorized to send for a domain. These extensions address SMTP's original security gaps.
